documents.unit: The Institute for Learning and Teaching (TILT), Academic Integrity
documents.title: NavigateAI Use at CSU: What's allowed, When to ask, and What to avoid
documents.summary: Student-facing TILT guide sorting AI uses into three zones: open learning uses, uses that need the instructor's explicit permission, and uses that count as academic misconduct. It also gives integrity FAQs, mostly not AI-specific.
documents.stance_why: The page sets three zones in its own words: 'Explore Freely' for learning uses, 'Permit Required Ahead' where 'Using AI for any work you get credit for requires their explicit permission', and 'Trail Closed'. Each instructor decides case by case ('Every guide runs their trail differently'), so the document is tiered and delegates to instructors.

units.why: The framing sentence sorts uses into "open", "special permits" and "closed" paths; it is a policy because it defines named tiers of AI use, so P05 (tiers) and not P04.
units.anchor: Some paths are open to everyone, some require special permits, and some are closed
units.frag_end: some are closed because the paths are perilous.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this lead-in sentence ('Some paths are open to everyone, some require special permits, and some are closed'). It states that AI uses are sorted into three named zones, which is a real tiering statement (P05) and appears nowhere else as a single statement. Kept as actor admin, phase general, informs.

units.why: 'You are encouraged to use AI as your personal guide for learning and discovery' opens the Trail Open zone and encourages students to use AI for study, understanding and exploring, which is the tutor use (P12) rather than a campus-wide default (P02); it is addressed to students doing coursework, so phase during-work, modality should.
units.anchor: You are encouraged to use AI as your personal guide for learning and discovery.
units.resolution_why: A coded P02 (default permit/encourage) with phase general; B coded P12 with phase during-work. The sentence sits in the 'Trail Open' zone only, and the next lines list study uses (explain a topic, explore concepts, practice questions). The document's default for credit work is the opposite (permission required), so P02 would misstate it. Final: P12, during-work, should, encourage.

units.why: 'Use AI to explain a complex topic from class in a new way' lists an always-acceptable use; using AI as a tutor to understand concepts is P12.
units.anchor: Use AI to explain a complex topic from class in a new way

units.why: Asking AI for key figures or main debates is exploring concepts, like a search engine or tutor, listed as 'always acceptable'; P12 not P15 because it is about learning content, not generating ideas for one's work.
units.anchor: Explore concepts related to your course.

units.why: 'Create practice questions or flashcards to study for an exam' is a study-aid use declared always acceptable (P14).
units.anchor: Create practice questions or flashcards to study for an exam

units.why: The warning that AI 'can sometimes lead you astray with wrong information (hallucinations)' states that output may be wrong, a fact supporting verification (P31).
units.anchor: AI tools can sometimes lead you astray with wrong information (hallucinations).

units.why: 'You are always responsible for verifying the facts and the quality of your work' obliges students to check AI output; P31 chosen over P29 because the context is hallucination.
units.anchor: You are always responsible for verifying the facts and the quality of your work.

units.why: "Using AI for any work you get credit for requires their explicit permission" sets a restrict-unless-permitted default; P06 (explicit allowance needed, otherwise not allowed) fits best, not P04 since it is the default itself.
units.anchor: Using AI for any work you get credit for requires their explicit permission.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on every code except phase: A general, B during-work. The sentence says 'Using AI for any work you get credit for requires their explicit permission', a rule about doing coursework, not a definition or scope statement. Final phase: during-work.

units.why: 'Getting a "permit" means asking your instructor if, and how, you can use AI for a specific assignment' defines the permission step: before using AI on credit work, students ask the instructor. That is the ask-first rule (P10); the per-instructor variation is coded separately under P04. The preceding sentence says students 'must stop and get a permit', so the rule is binding.
units.anchor: asking your instructor if, and how, you can use AI for a specific assignment
units.policy: Students must get a "permit" before using AI on credit work, which means asking their instructor if, and how, they can use AI for a specific assignment.
units.resolution_why: A coded should/P10/restrict; B coded informs/P04/neutral. The source defines the permit as asking the instructor, immediately after 'you must stop and get a permit from your trail guide', so the content is an ask-first requirement (P10), not the 'instructor decides' principle (P04, already coded from 'Every guide runs their trail differently'). B's informs misses the 'must' of the previous sentence. Final: must, P10, restrict, with a normalized policy.

units.why: 'Every guide runs their trail differently' says each instructor decides how AI may be used, so P04.
units.anchor: Every guide runs their trail differently.
units.resolution_why: A coded actor all, phase general; B coded actor student, phase course-start. The sentence 'Every guide runs their trail differently' is a fact that instructors set their own rules, not an instruction to students or a communication step. It matches the FAQ sentence 'the instructor of a course decides', which both coders coded all/general. Final: all, general, informs, P04.

units.why: Writing or co-authoring graded essays, reports or papers needs instructor sign-off ("Check with your instructor before using AI"); this is a prose rule so P18 over P04.
units.anchor: Write or co-author any part of a graded essay, lab report, or paper.
units.policy: Students check with their instructor before using AI to write or co-author any part of a graded essay, lab report, or paper.

units.why: Outlining or organizing arguments for a graded assignment needs prior instructor permission; a writing-process rule, so P18.
units.anchor: Outline or organize your arguments for a graded assignment.
units.policy: Students check with their instructor before using AI to outline or organize their arguments for a graded assignment.

units.why: "Generate code or solve problems for credit" is on the check-with-instructor list; AI code is allowed only if the instructor permits, which is P16 (conditional AI code), not P19, since it is not flatly banned.
units.anchor: Generate code or solve problems for credit.
units.policy: Students check with their instructor before using AI to generate code or solve problems for credit.

units.why: "Complete any portion of a take-home quiz, exam, or assignment" requires instructor permission; it is a take-home assessment rule decided by the instructor, so P04 rather than P22 (which bans in-class AI).
units.anchor: Complete any portion of a take-home quiz, exam, or assignment.
units.policy: Students check with their instructor before using AI to complete any portion of a take-home quiz, exam, or assignment.

units.why: 'When in doubt, ask your guide' directs students unsure about a use to ask the instructor (P10).
units.anchor: When in doubt, ask your guide.

units.why: 'An unauthorized trip here is considered academic misconduct' classifies unpermitted AI use in the permit-required zone as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: An unauthorized trip here is considered academic misconduct.
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed except unit_stance: A neutral, B restrict. 'An unauthorized trip here is considered academic misconduct' says that AI use in the permit zone without permission is misconduct, so it takes a restricting position, not only a definition. Final: restrict (P36, informs).

units.why: 'Entering it is a violation of CSU's Academic Integrity Policy' treats the closed uses as integrity violations, P36.
units.anchor: Entering it is a violation of CSU’s Academic Integrity Policy

units.why: 'This applies to anything considered work for credit (graded, pass/fail, or marked as completed)' defines the scope of the closed-trail rules (P61).
units.anchor: anything considered “work for credit” (graded, pass/fail, or marked as completed)
units.resolution_why: A coded actor all, B coded actor student. 'This applies to anything considered work for credit' sets the scope of the closed-trail rule that binds students' own graded work. Final: student, general, informs, P61.

units.why: 'Turning in an essay, lab report, or any other assignment that was fully generated by an AI' is banned: students may not have AI produce submitted work (P19).
units.anchor: any other assignment that was fully generated by an AI.
units.policy: Turning in an essay, lab report, or any other assignment fully generated by an AI is academic misconduct.

units.why: 'Using an AI tool in any way to answer questions during a quiz or exam' is a flat exam ban, P22.
units.anchor: Using an AI tool in any way to answer questions during a quiz or exam.
units.policy: Using an AI tool in any way to answer questions during a quiz or exam is academic misconduct.

units.why: 'Including fake sources, data, or citations that an AI made up in a research paper or bibliography' is listed as misconduct. The failing is submitting AI output without checking it, so the unit is filed under verify AI output (P31); P19 (do not have AI produce submitted work) is not chosen because the rule is about fabricated content, not AI authorship.
units.anchor: Including fake sources, data, or citations that an AI made up
units.resolution_why: A coded P19, B coded P31. P19 covers submitting AI-generated work as one's own, which is the separate 'Submitting a complete work' item. This item forbids fabricated content that AI invented, i.e. unverified hallucinated output, which the Hiker's Wisdom text ('hallucinations... responsible for verifying') ties to P31. Final: P31, must-not, prohibit.

units.why: 'Using AI to rewrite or "spin" sentences or paragraphs from a source and presenting them as your own original summary' forbids presenting AI-produced text as one's own work, which is P19; P18 (prose handled separately from code) is not chosen because the rule is about passing off AI text as own, not a prose-versus-code distinction.
units.anchor: Using AI to rewrite or “spin” sentences or paragraphs from a source
units.resolution_why: A coded P19, B coded P18. The passage forbids AI rewriting a source and 'presenting them as your own', i.e. having AI produce text you submit as yours (P19). P18 is for rules that treat prose differently from code, which this does not do. Final: P19.

units.why: 'Intentionally hiding your use of AI on an assignment where your instructor has explicitly asked you to declare it' makes nondisclosure the violation (P28).
units.anchor: Intentionally hiding your use of AI on an assignment

units.why: 'Submitting AI-generated code, formulas, or solutions and claiming them as your own work' is misconduct; P19 covers code and solutions presented as own.
units.anchor: Submitting AI-generated code, formulas, or solutions and claiming them as your own work

units.why: The helicopter analogy and 'building the strength and skill that only come from the climb' explain that the learning process, not the answer, is the goal, so P41.
units.anchor: building the strength and skill that only come from the climb

units.why: 'How do I credit my AI Tools (when allowed)? Visit the CSU Library's AI Citation Guide' points students to citation guidance, so P24 as a pointer to how to cite AI use.
units.anchor: How do I credit my AI Tools (when allowed)?
units.policy: Students are directed to the CSU Library's AI Citation Guide for how to credit AI tools when AI use is allowed.

units.why: 'We used a large language model as a collaborative partner to help brainstorm analogies, refine the language, and structure the content' is the Academic Integrity Program disclosing that the guide itself was made with AI. That is disclosure of AI-made materials (P48); P47 (instructor use disclosed to students) fits less well because the content is a published resource, not grading or feedback.
units.anchor: We used a large language model as a collaborative partner
units.resolution_why: A coded P48, B coded P47. The note discloses that the published guide was drafted with a language model, which matches P48 (course materials created with AI are disclosed). P47 is about instructors describing their own AI use in grading, feedback or demos. Final: P48.

units.why: 'The instructor of a course decides what is acceptable and unacceptable help' gives the instructor authority over assistance rules, P04.
units.anchor: the instructor of a course decides what is acceptable and unacceptable help

units.why: 'The expectation can change from course to course' says help rules (including collaboration) do not carry across courses (P11); P04 covers who decides, so this clause goes to P11.
units.anchor: the expectation can change from course to course

documents.unit: The Institute for Learning and Teaching (TILT)
documents.title: Crafting Syllabus Statements on Generative Artificial Intelligence Use
documents.summary: TILT faculty guidance on writing short generative-AI syllabus statements, with four sample statements and advice on teaching AI literacies. It states that a campus umbrella policy is unlikely to fit and leaves choices to instructors.
documents.stance_why: The guide offers templates ('Below are several examples you can adopt or adapt') ranging from prohibitive to permissive, and says 'it seems unlikely that a campus umbrella policy will satisfy the many needs', so it sets no stance itself and delegates to instructors.

units.why: "They guide: they clarify expectations and help prevent misunderstanding" gives the purpose of syllabus statements; a push to state AI expectations in the syllabus, P09.
units.anchor: they clarify expectations and help prevent misunderstanding
units.resolution_why: Only B coded 'they clarify expectations and help prevent misunderstanding'. It states the purpose of AI syllabus statements; it is a real rationale for the statement requirement, kept as informs under P09, before-course.

units.why: "When something undesirable occurs... they are what we point to as the stated expectation" says statements back later enforcement; P09 fits as the reason to write them.
units.anchor: they are what we point to as the stated expectation of the course
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on codes except phase: A course-start, B before-course. 'they are what we point to as the stated expectation of the course' explains why the instructor writes the statement; it is statement-design rationale, so before-course.

units.why: "Syllabus statements should aim for clarity and brevity" directs instructors on how to communicate AI rules: P09.
units.anchor: Syllabus statements should aim for
units.resolution_why: Only B coded 'Syllabus statements should aim for clarity and brevity'. It is a direct instruction to instructors on how to write the statement, so a real policy statement (should, P09, before-course).

units.why: The guide says students 'should immediately understand whether they are allowed to use AI', a recommendation that syllabi state AI rules (P09).
units.anchor: Students should immediately understand whether they are allowed to use AI
units.resolution_why: A coded phase before-course, B coded course-start. 'Students should immediately understand whether they are allowed to use AI' is guidance on how an instructor should write the statement, i.e. design work done before the course. Final: before-course.

units.why: 'Does it cover all course activities or only graded work?' tells instructors to state the policy's scope in the statement (P09).
units.anchor: Does it cover all course activities or only graded work?
units.policy: An AI syllabus statement should say whether the policy covers all course activities or only graded work.

units.why: 'State clearly what students are allowed and not allowed to do' asks instructors to spell out permitted and prohibited uses in the syllabus (P09).
units.anchor: State clearly what students are allowed and not allowed to do.
units.resolution_why: Only A coded 'State clearly what students are allowed and not allowed to do'. It is the second of the four questions an ideal statement should answer, a distinct recommendation to instructors. Kept as should, P09, before-course.

units.why: 'If you plan to use a clarifying resource, a color-coded chart or other guide, reference it here' recommends tiered frameworks, so P05.
units.anchor: a color-coded chart or other guide, reference it here

units.why: 'Encourage dialogue by inviting students to talk with you' has the statement tell students where to take questions, which supports asking the instructor (P10).
units.anchor: Encourage dialogue by inviting students to talk with you.

units.why: The prohibitive sample says 'You may NOT use AI when completing any assignments, assessments, or other work for credit', a default ban on credit work (P01).
units.anchor: You may NOT use AI when completing any assignments, assessments, or other work for credit

units.why: The same sample says 'You MAY use it to investigate, study, summarize, etc. course material', permitting AI as a study aid; P12 since it is about understanding material.
units.anchor: You MAY use it to investigate, study, summarize, etc. course material

units.why: The sample refers to 'a color-coded framework that we will be using to help make this distinction clearer', a tiered scheme (P05).
units.anchor: Here is a color-coded framework that we will be using

units.why: 'You may only use generative AI in this class in specific ways' is the sample conditional statement's rule: AI is allowed only for specified uses. That is a default of restriction with permission by exception, closest to P06; the per-assignment mechanism is coded in the next units under P04.
units.anchor: You may only use generative AI in this class in specific ways.
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this sentence ('You may only use generative AI in this class in specific ways'). It is a rule in the sample Conditional statement, not covered by any A unit. Kept, template wording addressed to students; P06 (default restriction unless permitted) with must and restrict.

units.why: The conditional sample uses 'a color-coded framework to make it clear HOW you can use AI and WHEN you can use it', a tiered scheme (P05); the per-assignment discussion is coded as P04 in the next unit.
units.anchor: I will use a color-coded framework to make it clear HOW you can use AI
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on codes except unit_stance: A restrict, B neutral. 'I will use a color-coded framework to make it clear HOW you can use AI and WHEN' announces a communication tool and takes no position on AI use. Final: neutral, P05, informs.

units.why: 'We will discuss how you may use AI on each course assignment or assessment at the time it is introduced' sets AI rules per assignment (P04).
units.anchor: how you may use AI on each course assignment or assessment
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed except unit_stance: A restrict, B neutral. 'we will discuss how you may use AI on each course assignment or assessment' describes a per-assignment conversation and sets no position itself. Final: neutral, P04, informs.

units.why: 'You are not authorized to use artificial intelligence to produce work for this class except on assignments that I have explicitly identified' bans AI by default with permission only where the instructor names the assignment. That is the fallback-rule type (P06: unless explicitly allowed, AI is prohibited); P04 is not chosen because the sentence sets the default, and who identifies the exceptions is secondary.
units.anchor: You are not authorized to use artificial intelligence to produce work for this class
units.policy: Students are not authorized to use artificial intelligence to produce work for the class except on assignments the instructor has explicitly identified.
units.resolution_why: A anchored the exception clause and coded P04; B anchored the prohibition and coded P06. Both are the same sentence. The sentence sets a default ban with exceptions the instructor names, which matches P06's example ('unless explicitly allowed, AI is prohibited'). Final: P06, must-not, restrict, with a normalized policy that includes the exception.

units.why: 'On those assignments, you will receive significant guidance on the appropriate use of such technologies' commits the instructor to give assignment-level guidance where AI is allowed. It belongs under the per-assignment rule (P04); P35 (redesign assignments around AI) is not chosen because no assignment redesign is stated. It takes no stance beyond the exception already coded.
units.anchor: you will receive significant guidance on the appropriate use of such technologies
units.resolution_why: A coded P35/neutral, B coded P04/permit. The sentence promises guidance on the assignments where AI is permitted; it does not redesign assessment (P35) and the permission itself is in the preceding exception clause. Final: P04, neutral.

units.why: 'You may not construe this limited permission as approval to use these technologies in any other facet of this course' keeps permission to the named assignments (P11).
units.anchor: You may not construe this limited permission as approval

units.why: 'The use of generative AI tools is broadly permitted in this course to help you brainstorm, draft, and revise your work' is a permissive default (P02).
units.anchor: generative AI tools is broadly permitted in this course

units.why: 'You are fully accountable for the final submission' makes students own what they submit (P29).
units.anchor: you are fully accountable for the final submission

units.why: 'Fact-check all AI-generated content for accuracy' requires verifying AI output (P31).
units.anchor: Fact-check all AI-generated content for accuracy.

units.why: 'Revise all content to ensure it meets assignment requirements and reflects your own understanding' is listed among what students are 'required to' do. It makes the student responsible for the submitted work's quality and ownership, so P29; P32 (student stays primary problem-solver) is not chosen because the sentence is about the final submission, not the process.
units.anchor: Revise all content to ensure it meets assignment requirements
units.policy: Students must revise all AI-generated content to ensure it meets assignment requirements and reflects their own understanding.
units.resolution_why: A anchored 'reflects your own understanding' and coded P32; B anchored the whole instruction and coded P29. Both are one requirement in the Accountability sample. It follows 'you are fully accountable for the final submission' and asks that the submission be revised and reflect the student's understanding: ownership of the submission (P29). Final: P29, with a normalized policy.

units.why: 'Cite your use of the AI tool following the guidance in the CSU Library's Guidelines' requires citing AI use (P24).
units.anchor: Cite your use of the AI tool

units.why: 'Submitting inaccurate or unedited AI-generated work ... will result in a poor grade' states a consequence in advance (P37).
units.anchor: Submitting inaccurate or unedited AI-generated work fails to meet the standards for academic integrity
units.frag_end: will result in a poor grade.
units.policy: Submitting inaccurate or unedited AI-generated work fails to meet the standards for academic integrity and will result in a poor grade.

units.why: 'Teach students how to use generative AI tools effectively' asks faculty to build functional AI skills, a professional skill (P44).
units.anchor: Teach students how to use generative AI tools effectively

units.why: 'Encourage students to evaluate AI's strengths, weaknesses, assumptions, and societal impacts' is one of the three literacies instructors are advised to teach. It belongs with the other AI-literacy bullets (P44, teach AI use as a skill); P31 (students verify output) is not chosen because it is about teaching critical evaluation, and P53 is not chosen because it does not itself name harms.
units.anchor: Encourage students to evaluate AI’s strengths, weaknesses, assumptions, and societal impacts
units.resolution_why: A coded P31, B coded P53. The sentence advises instructors to build critical literacy about AI, one of three literacies that A and B both filed under P44 (teach effective AI use). It does not tell students to verify output (P31) or list harms (P53). Final: P44, should, encourage.

units.why: 'Guide students to assess when and how to use AI in different contexts' is teaching judgment about effective AI use (P44).
units.anchor: Guide students to assess when and how to use AI in different contexts

units.why: The further-reading list is offered "to expand their understanding of generative AI and how to prepare their courses": support for faculty learning, P63.
units.anchor: expand their understanding of generative AI and how to prepare their courses
units.resolution_why: Only B coded 'expand their understanding of generative AI and how to prepare their courses', the lead-in to the Further Reading resources for faculty. It is a real statement of faculty support resources, kept as P63.

units.why: The closing names 'academic integrity and critical thinking, environmental impact, unevenly distributed access' as concerns, so P53; access is mentioned but the passage mainly names harms.
units.anchor: environmental impact, unevenly distributed access,etc.
units.resolution_why: A coded actor all, B coded admin. 'environmental impact, unevenly distributed access' is a general acknowledgment of concerns, not an instruction to the university office. Final: all, general, informs, P53.

units.why: 'It seems unlikely that a campus umbrella policy will satisfy the many needs' states the university does not set one rule and leaves it to instructors (P04).
units.anchor: it seems unlikely that a campus umbrella policy will satisfy

units.why: 'You are urged to use your best judgment and to update your syllabus languages your ideas change' asks instructors to revise their statements, P54.
units.anchor: to update your syllabus languages your ideas change

units.why: 'Consider consulting the standards of your disciplinary community' advises faculty to look to outside norms before setting a course policy, closest to P63 (advice to learn before setting policy).
units.anchor: Consider consulting the standards of your disciplinary community

units.why: The closing question 'How am I ensuring that the use of AI in my course promotes an approach that reflects the higher order thinking' is advice to instructors to reflect before setting course policy. That matches P63 (advice that instructors consider implications before setting policy); P41 is not chosen because no rule limits AI to protect skill building.
units.anchor: promotes an approach that reflects the higher order thinking
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this closing question, as P41. It is a real recommendation to instructors (a self-check question), kept. The skill-building rationale of P41 is not stated; the passage is advice to instructors before setting course policy, so P63.

units.why: 'This resource was coauthored using generative AI (Ram-GPT) under the guidance of Colorado State University employees' discloses AI use in making a published resource. That is disclosure of AI-made materials (P48); P47 is for instructor use in grading, feedback or demos.
units.anchor: This resource was coauthored using generative AI (Ram-GPT)
units.resolution_why: A coded P48, B coded P47. The acknowledgment discloses that the guidance page itself was drafted with AI and reviewed by CSU employees, matching P48. Final: P48.

notes: No school, computing-unit or course documents were collected (course layer deferred). Only the two TILT university-layer documents were coded. NavigateAI FAQ sections on cheating, plagiarism, study-guide sites, self-plagiarism, falsification and facilitation are not AI-specific and were not coded, except the sentences that the instructor decides acceptable help. Sample statements in the syllabus guide are templates addressed to students; their unit_stance reflects the sample text, not a CSU rule. The NavigateAI page repeats its three trail sections twice; anchors are taken from the first occurrence.
